planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed above 60°F; a compact bush dry bean that needs no staking and is left on the plant until pods rattle and dry down in late summer.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm garden soil in rows spaced 24 to 30 inches apart, since this upright bush variety needs no trellising. Lina Sisco's Bird Egg is a Missouri family heirloom, carried west from the Ozarks in the 1880s and shared through Seed Savers Exchange, prized for its off-white seeds splashed with maroon streaks that resemble a speckled bird's egg. The dry beans cook up with a creamy, almost potato-like texture and mild flavor that holds up well in soups and baked bean dishes. Let pods dry fully on the plant before pulling the whole vine to finish curing indoors if fall rains threaten.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil has warmed above 60°F, next to a sturdy trellis, pole, or fence at least 6 feet tall for this vigorous climbing heirloom.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of poles or a trellis after the soil has warmed, thinning to one strong seedling per pole or every 6 to 9 inches along a fence. Garden of Eden is a dual-purpose heirloom pole bean, grown from seed stock originating in Iberia, that produces broad, flat, deep-green pods up to 7 inches long that stay tender and sweet even as they size up. Pick young for a mild snap bean, or let pods mature and dry fully on the vine to harvest light brown, darkly striped seeds for a rich shell or dry bean. Keep vines picked regularly through the 6 to 8 week harvest window to encourage continued pod set.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed above 60°F; an upright, self-supporting bush bean that needs no staking and dries down for harvest in early fall.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in rows 24 to 30 inches apart in warm, fertile soil; this compact, upright bush selection holds its pods well off the ground for easier hand or mechanical harvest. Midnight Black Turtle Soup traces to a small black bean brought into the United States in the early 1800s and later refined into a tidy, heavy-yielding bush strain long grown for classic black bean soup. The small, glossy black seeds cook down creamy and rich while holding their shape, making them a favorite for soups, stews, and Latin-style rice and beans. Pull entire plants once most pods have dried and rattle, then finish curing indoors before shelling.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost against a tall, sturdy trellis or pole structure; this vigorous climbing runner bean performs best where summer nights stay cool.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of a tall trellis, teepee, or fence once the soil has warmed, since vines can climb 8 to 10 feet and need sturdy support. White Emergo is a long-grown heirloom runner bean valued for its cream-white blossoms, smooth stringless green pods 8 to 12 inches long, and creamy white seeds that can be eaten as a fresh snap bean, shelled green as a butterbean, or dried for winter storage. It has earned recognition from the Royal Horticultural Society for its reliable, heavy yields and fine flavor. Keep pods picked regularly to extend the harvest and prevent the plant from slowing production.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil has warmed above 60°F, next to a tall pole or trellis for this vigorous Appalachian climbing heirloom.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of poles or a trellis once soil has warmed, allowing the vigorous vines room to climb 6 to 8 feet. Tennessee Cutshort is one of the classic Appalachian "greasy" and cutshort pole beans kept alive by mountain seed savers, named for the way its pods pack so tightly with brown seeds that the bean ends square off against one another inside the pod. Pods can be snapped and cooked fresh while still tender, or left to dry fully on the vine for a flavorful soup bean later in the season. Pick frequently during the fresh-eating stage to keep plants productive through a long harvest window.
